items.context: The workspace needs a Zustand store for graph state (nodes, edges, selection, layout mode, highlight/dim/hide, viewport, lens, filters). The current codebase has 6 separate single-concern stores. The graph workspace could use one unified graph store or split into focused slices (e.g., graphDataStore for nodes/edges, graphUIStore for selection/highlight/viewport). A single store is simpler but risks becoming a god store; split stores add indirection but follow the existing codebase pattern of small focused stores.

options.label: Single unified graph store
options.rationale: One store for all graph state (nodes, edges, selection, layout, viewport, filters). Simpler cross-cutting updates (e.g., selecting a node updates both highlight state and viewport). Matches how prompt-manager structures its graph store. Risk: can grow large as lenses add state.

options.label: Split into graph-data + graph-ui stores
options.rationale: graphDataStore owns nodes/edges/lens/filters (data-driven). graphUIStore owns selectedNode/highlightState/layoutMode/viewport (interaction-driven). Follows the existing codebase pattern of small focused stores. Cleaner separation — data fetching doesn't trigger UI re-renders. Recommended because the react-coherence skill advises against god stores and the existing codebase already uses this pattern.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own store architecture approach.

items.topic: Sidebar feed data source and architecture
items.context: The sidebar needs an activity-first unified feed with entity-type filter toggles. The existing `lib/feed.ts` already generates a smart feed with attention reasons (needs_review, stale, blocked, high_priority, etc.) from the backlog store. It could be extended to include captures, scenarios, and execution records. Alternatively, a new feed mechanism could be built from scratch for the sidebar context.

options.label: Extend existing feed.ts with multi-entity support
options.rationale: Builds on proven attention-reason logic already in production. Add capture, scenario, and execution feed items alongside backlog items. Reuses the sorting/prioritization logic. Recommended because it avoids duplication and the existing feed logic is well-structured.

options.label: New sidebar-specific feed module
options.rationale: Clean-slate feed optimized for the sidebar context. Can model feed items as a unified type from the start rather than retrofitting. More freedom in how items are ranked and filtered. Risk: duplicates existing attention-reason logic.

items.context: Settings and Prompts currently occupy primary tabs. They need to move behind the gear icon. The question is how to present them — a single drawer with sections, separate drawers, or a modal dialog. The current SettingsPage is 28.7KB and PromptsPage is 36.7KB, both substantial components.

options.label: Single settings drawer with tabbed sections (Settings + Prompts)
options.rationale: One gear icon → one drawer with internal tabs for Settings and Prompts. Simplest mental model for users. Keeps both accessible from the same entry point. Recommended because it reduces UI surface area and groups low-frequency actions together.

options.label: Gear icon opens Settings modal; Prompts moved to inspector context
options.rationale: Settings gets a modal. Prompts become contextual — shown in the inspector when viewing execution records or backlog items that reference prompts. More discoverable in context but loses the standalone browse capability.

options.label: Gear icon dropdown menu with separate entry points
options.rationale: Gear icon shows a small dropdown: 'Settings' and 'Prompts' as separate entries, each opening its own full drawer/modal. Preserves them as distinct experiences. Slightly more clicks but cleaner separation.

items.topic: Component organization for the graph workspace
items.context: The graph workspace is a substantial new surface with ~10-15 new components (GraphWorkspace, GraphCanvas, Sidebar, SidebarFeed, Inspector, InspectorPopover, InspectorBottomSheet, Header, LensSwitcher, LayoutModePicker, etc.). The current codebase uses a flat components/ directory with component-per-file. The react-coherence skill recommends a surfaces/ pattern for feature assembly. This is a good opportunity to establish structure for the new workspace without refactoring existing code.

options.label: New surfaces/graph/ directory following react-coherence pattern
options.rationale: Create `src/surfaces/graph/` with subdirectories: `components/`, `hooks/`, `stores/`. Keeps graph workspace self-contained. Follows the react-coherence recommended structure. Shared primitives stay in existing locations. Recommended because it establishes a clean pattern for the new major surface without disrupting existing code.

options.label: Flat additions to existing components/ directory
options.rationale: Add graph components alongside existing ones in `src/components/`. Consistent with current codebase style. Simpler — no new directory conventions to learn. Risk: components/ becomes crowded with 40+ files mixing graph and non-graph concerns.

items.topic: Graph data bootstrapping strategy for the shell
items.context: This item builds the shell frame, but the graph-data-foundation API endpoint doesn't exist yet (separate execute item). The shell needs some data to render a functional graph canvas. The question is how to bootstrap data before the dedicated graph API is ready.

options.label: Assemble graph data client-side from existing stores and APIs
options.rationale: Use existing backlog, scenarios, execution, and capture stores/services to construct a temporary client-side graph model. Map store data into React Flow nodes/edges format. This is throwaway code that gets replaced when the graph API lands, but it makes the shell immediately functional and testable. Recommended because it unblocks the shell from the API dependency and provides real data for integration testing.

options.label: Use hardcoded stub data only
options.rationale: Render the shell with static placeholder nodes and edges. No real data integration until the graph API is ready. Simplest approach — zero throwaway code. Risk: shell can't be validated with real data patterns until the API item completes.
